entries.narration: Before we look at a single Snowflake feature, let's look at the problem it is meant to solve. Throughout this course we follow one retailer. Orders arrive from an application database, customer details change in a CRM, and a small set of reference data describes products and stores. Our job is to turn those into a trusted analytical data product: clean order details, plus business summaries built on top of them. The interesting part is that the people reading it do not want the same thing. The finance team looks at yesterday's revenue each morning, so a daily refresh is fine, but the numbers must reconcile to the cent. A customer-facing app wants order status within minutes. Analysts want to ask questions nobody planned for. So we carry four requirements with us. Freshness: how stale is acceptable, and for whom. Correctness: what one row means, and how totals are defined. Cost: what we pay for compute, for storage, and for automation that runs on its own. And ownership: who decides what revenue means, and who answers when it is wrong. Every later choice, from how we load data to how we schedule it, is a trade between these four.

Snowflake is built from three layers, and the separation between them explains a lot of its behaviour. At the bottom is database storage. When you load a table, Snowflake reorganises the data into compressed, columnar files called micro-partitions, and it also keeps the historical versions it needs for features like Time Travel. In the middle is compute: virtual warehouses, which are clusters of machines that actually execute your queries. Because compute is separate from storage, a warehouse can be started, stopped or resized without moving any data, and two warehouses can read the same tables at the same time without copying anything. At the top sits cloud services, which authenticates you, plans each query using metadata about those micro-partitions, and checks whether your role is allowed to do what you asked. Snowflake runs all three for you: there are no servers to patch and no disks to manage. But notice what is still yours. Whether the data that loads is correct, what revenue means, which role may see which column, and how much compute you run and when. A managed platform will faithfully execute any SQL you give it, including SQL that is wrong.

Every query we run happens inside an account, so it's worth knowing where an account lives. A company's accounts sit together under an organisation. Each account is created on one cloud platform, such as AWS, Azure or Google Cloud, and in one Snowflake Region within that cloud. That choice decides where your data is physically stored and processed, which matters for regulation, for latency, and for cost, because moving data between Regions or clouds is billed. Each account also has an edition. Standard is the entry point, Enterprise adds features such as multi-cluster warehouses and longer Time Travel, Business Critical adds stronger security and compliance options along with failover, and Virtual Private Snowflake runs in its own isolated environment. In our retailer's organisation, production runs on Enterprise in a US Region, a European account on Azure runs Business Critical, and a development account stays on Standard. Clients find an account by its identifier: the organisation name, a hyphen, and the account name, because an account name on its own is only unique inside its organisation. You will still meet older URLs built from an account locator, which embed the Region and cloud in the hostname; they work, but the organisation form is the one to prefer. The habit to build now is simple. When you read any example, including the ones in this course, check which cloud, Region and edition it assumes.

When you connect to Snowflake, you open a session, and that session carries context. There are four pieces worth watching. The current role decides which privileges apply, so the same statement can succeed for one role and be denied for another. The current warehouse decides which compute will execute your query. And the current database and schema decide how a short name like orders is resolved into a full table name. Anything you don't set explicitly falls back to the user's defaults, which can differ from one user to the next, so the same script can behave differently for two people. The word warehouse trips up many newcomers, because in most of the industry a data warehouse is where data lives. In Snowflake, a virtual warehouse is only compute. It stores no tables at all. It reads and writes the shared storage layer, and when it is suspended, your data is exactly where it was. That separation is what gives you workload isolation. Our retailer runs a small warehouse for dashboards and a medium one for the nightly load. Both read the same tables, but because they are separate compute, a heavy load cannot make the finance dashboard wait behind it. Each warehouse has its own size and its own auto-suspend and auto-resume settings, which, as we'll see shortly, is also where most compute cost is decided.

Let's run a first query. In Snowsight, the browser interface, you would type it into a worksheet. From code, the Snowflake CLI, a driver, or a connector sends exactly the same SQL; each simply opens a session first. The first two lines set that session's context explicitly. We use the analyst role, so that role's privileges apply, and the B I warehouse, so that warehouse's compute does the work. Then comes the query. Notice that the table is named in full: the retail database, the sales schema, the orders table. A fully qualified name doesn't depend on whatever database and schema the session happens to be using, which makes the query safe to copy into another worksheet or script. The where clause keeps the five orders from the first of October and drops the one from the second. Group by order status then collapses those five rows into one row per status, and we count orders and sum their totals. Finally, order by sorts by revenue. Without it, Snowflake makes no promise about row order, so never rely on the order you happened to see. Every run also gets a query ID, which is the handle we'll use later to find the query in history and open its profile. Don't just accept the result; check it. The three shipped orders add up to two hundred and twelve forty. Also notice the column names come back in upper case, because Snowflake stores unquoted identifiers that way. And the result has one row per status, because that is the grain we grouped by.

Cost in Snowflake is easier to reason about once you split it into kinds. The biggest is usually warehouse compute. A warehouse consumes credits per hour according to its size, and each size step roughly doubles the rate. A small standard warehouse uses two credits an hour, a medium uses four. Billing is per second, but every time a warehouse starts or resumes, you pay for at least one minute. Cloud services, the layer that plans queries and checks privileges, is only billed on days when it exceeds ten percent of your warehouse usage. Serverless features, such as Snowpipe or serverless tasks, are metered separately, because Snowflake supplies their compute rather than one of your warehouses. And storage is billed on the average amount kept on disk across the month, including history kept for recovery. So the habit is to write the assumptions down. Our dashboard warehouse is small, runs about six hours on twenty-two working days: two hundred and sixty-four credits. The nightly load is medium for half an hour every day: sixty credits. Those are estimates you can check later against real usage. Finally, separate lifecycle from data. A suspended warehouse costs nothing and loses only its cache. Even dropping a warehouse deletes compute, never a table.

Every Snowflake object has an address, and it helps to know which level of the tree it lives at. Tables, views and stages live inside a schema, and every schema lives inside a database. That gives each of them a three-part name: database, schema, object. Some objects are not stored in any database at all. Users, roles, warehouses and integrations belong to the account itself, so they are named with a single word. For the rest of the course, our retailer's data sits in one database called retail, with three schemas. Raw holds data exactly as it landed from the sources, including an orders table and a stage that points at cloud storage. Sales holds the cleaned data: orders, customers, and a daily revenue view. Reference holds products and stores. Each schema groups objects that share a lifecycle and an audience, which, as we'll see, makes access far easier to grant. Notice that raw and sales both contain a table called orders. That is deliberate and very common, because the landed copy and the cleaned copy are naturally called the same thing. A fully qualified name tells them apart without any doubt. A short name does not, and in the next section we will see exactly how that goes wrong.

When you write a short name like orders, Snowflake does not search the whole account for it. It resolves the name against the session's current database and schema. That makes the name only as reliable as the context it runs in. Here is the same statement, counting orders, run in two sessions. The first session is using the sales schema, so orders means the cleaned table, and the answer is six, one row per order. The second session happens to be using the raw schema, perhaps because its user's default was set that way, or because an earlier script changed it. Now orders means the landed table, which still contains three duplicate deliveries, and the answer is nine. Neither session sees an error. One of them simply gets a wrong number, and that is far harder to notice than a failure. Case adds a second trap. Unquoted identifiers are stored and matched in upper case, so orders, Orders and quoted upper-case ORDERS all reach the same table. A double-quoted identifier keeps its exact case, so quoted Orders with a capital O is a different object altogether. The habit that avoids both traps is simple: fully qualify the names in anything that runs without a person watching.

Every connection to Snowflake is made as a user, and a user is an identity, not a permission. Before that connection becomes a session, two checks happen. First a network policy, if one is set, decides whether the connection may come from where it is coming from. Then the user authenticates. Snowflake now draws a sharp line between two kinds of user. A person, such as our analyst Ana, is a user of type person. She signs in through single sign-on, or with a password plus multi-factor authentication. A workload, such as our nightly load job, is a user of type service. A service user cannot use a password at all, and cannot enrol in multi-factor authentication. Instead it proves who it is with a key pair, with workload identity federation, which lets a cloud workload use the identity its platform already gives it, or with a programmatic access token. An older type, legacy service, allowed passwords for automation; it is being retired and migrated to service. Two habits follow. A job never borrows a person's login; it gets its own user, so its access can be reviewed and revoked on its own. And a user's default role and warehouse only decide where a session starts. What it may do is decided by roles, which come next.

In Snowflake, privileges are granted to roles, and roles are granted to users. A person never holds a privilege directly. Roles can also be granted to other roles, and that is how a hierarchy forms: when you grant role A to role B, role B inherits everything role A can do. Our retailer has two working roles. Analyst reads the sales schema, and loader writes the raw schema. Both are granted to retail admin, which owns the retail database, and retail admin is granted to sysadmin, so the whole custom tree stays connected to the system roles that administer the account. At the top sits account admin. It is powerful, but it is not a magic superuser, and it should belong to a small number of people and never be anyone's default. At the bottom is public, which every user and role has automatically, so nothing sensitive should ever be granted to it. Inside a session, roles are active in two ways. The primary role is the one you set with use role, and it owns anything the session creates. Secondary roles, often all of the user's other roles, add their privileges to every other statement. The design principle running through all of this is least privilege: each role holds exactly what its job needs, and nothing more.

A query only runs if every link in a chain of privileges is in place. For our analyst to read the cleaned orders table, the analyst role needs usage on the retail database, usage on the sales schema, and select on the orders table itself. It also needs usage on a warehouse, because without compute nothing runs at all. The role matrix lays out the two working roles side by side. Both can read sales. Only loader can see the raw schema, where it inserts landed data, and each role uses its own warehouse. Now watch what happens when the analyst tries to count the raw orders. The error says the object does not exist or is not authorized. That wording is deliberate. Snowflake will not tell a role about objects it is not allowed to see, so a missing object and a missing grant look identical. Work through it in order: check the fully qualified name first, then show the grants to the role. Here the gap is usage on the raw schema, and it is there on purpose. Behind every grant is an owner. Each object is owned by exactly one role, which holds the ownership privilege and decides who else gets access. Here that is retail admin. Because ownership belongs to a role rather than a person, it survives people changing jobs. An owner can also grant a privilege with grant option, which lets the receiving role pass it on, and revoking a privilege from a role removes it at once for every user who holds that role.

So far every role has been an account role, which exists at the level of the whole account. Snowflake has a second kind: the database role. A database role is created inside one database, and it can only hold privileges on that database's objects. Our retail database gets two of them. Sales read holds usage on the sales schema and select on its tables. Raw write holds the privileges to land data in raw. Notice what a database role cannot do: it can never be the primary or a secondary role in a session. To use its privileges, you grant it to an account role, and granting it also implies usage on the database that contains it. So analyst receives sales read, and loader receives raw write. Why add another layer? There are two good reasons. First, delegation: whoever owns the retail database can shape access inside it, without needing rights to change account-wide roles. Second, portability: because the roles live inside the database, the access model travels with it, into clones, into replicas, and into shares, which we will meet in chapter nine; a consumer of a share grants its database roles to their own account roles. The hierarchy only runs one way, though: an account role can never be granted to a database role. The pattern that results is a small number of account roles, one per job, each assembled from database roles that describe access to specific data.

Once roles exist, the next question is who is allowed to hand out access. In an ordinary schema, the owner of each object makes that decision. If the loader role creates a table in raw, loader can grant select on it to anyone it likes, and over time those decisions scatter across many owners. A managed access schema changes the rule. Only the schema's owner, or a role holding the account-wide manage grants privilege, can grant access to the objects inside it. Object owners still own their objects, but they no longer decide who reads them. Our sales schema is managed in exactly this way. The second tool here is the future grant. Granting select on all tables covers the tables that exist today. Granting select on future tables tells Snowflake to apply the same grant to every table created in that schema from now on. It never reaches back to tables that already exist, which is why the two grants are usually issued together. So when a returns table appears next month, sales read can already query it, with no ticket and no forgotten grant. If future grants exist at both the database and the schema level for the same kind of object, the schema-level ones win. None of this removes the human part. Someone still owns the grant decisions for each schema, and grants never expire by themselves, so they need reviewing.

The last access boundary sits at the edge of Snowflake, where data comes from, or goes to, your own cloud storage. Say the loader needs to read files from an S3 bucket. That request crosses three separate permission systems, and any one of them can refuse it. Inside Snowflake, the loader role needs usage on the landing stage. Whoever creates that stage also needs usage on a storage integration. The integration is an account-level object that holds the AWS role Snowflake should use and a list of allowed locations, so even a stage cannot point anywhere it likes. Then the request leaves Snowflake. On the AWS side, Snowflake acts as an IAM user, one for the whole account, which assumes the IAM role you created. That role's trust policy names Snowflake's user and an external ID, and you copy both from describe integration. Recreate the integration without fixing the external ID and the trust breaks. Network policies guard the inbound direction. They limit where connections may come from, a policy set on a user overrides the account's policy, and a refused connection never reaches authentication at all. Access, then, is layered: names, identities, roles, privileges, and cloud permissions. With those boundaries in place, we can turn to the data itself, and to how tables behave when they change.

Let's start this chapter with the table itself, because a table is a promise about its rows. Every column in our cleaned orders table makes one. The order ID is always present and identifies exactly one order. The order date is a real date. The total is an amount of money with two decimal places. The status is one of a small set of values. Before any data loads, it pays to write those promises down, along with what will actually keep each one when a source system misbehaves. The cheapest guard is the data type. Money goes in an exact number type with fixed decimals, not a floating-point one that rounds. Dates go in date and timestamp types, never in text columns. Then a bad value fails at the door. Try to insert the text N A into a numeric column and the statement is rejected immediately. Put the same text in a varchar column and it loads without a murmur, then breaks a sum in next week's report, far from where it came from. Not null is the next guard, and Snowflake enforces it. But notice that one row per order is a promise no type can keep by itself. Something has to check it, and the next section shows why that something is usually you.

Snowflake lets you declare the usual constraints on a table, but on a standard table only some of them are enforced. Not null is enforced, and so is check, which tests a condition on each row. Primary key, unique and foreign key are recorded, visible to tools, and then not enforced at all. Let's see what that means for orders. We declare order ID as the primary key and add a check that the total is never negative. Now insert a second row for order one thousand and one. It loads without any complaint, because the primary key is informational. Insert an order with a total of minus five, and the check fails, taking the whole statement with it. If you need keys that are truly enforced, hybrid tables enforce them, and we'll meet those at the end of the chapter. So why declare keys on a standard table? They document the model for people and for BI tools. And with the rely property, you tell the optimizer that the key really holds, which lets it skip unnecessary joins. Use that carefully: a rely key that is false produces wrong answers, not errors. The practical rule is that you keep the promise yourself. Deduplicate before loading, and run a duplicate check afterwards, like the group by query at the bottom of the scene.

When you create a table, you also choose how long it remembers. Snowflake has three kinds. A permanent table lives until it is dropped, and it keeps history in two stages. First comes Time Travel, a retention period you set, from zero up to ninety days on Enterprise edition, with a default of one day. During that window, you can query old versions, clone them, and undrop the table. After Time Travel ends, changed and dropped data spends seven more days in Fail-safe. Fail-safe is not something you query. It is a last-resort recovery that only Snowflake can perform. Then the data is gone. A transient table also lives until dropped, but it has at most one day of Time Travel and no Fail-safe at all. A temporary table is like a transient one, but it belongs to a single session: no other session can see it, and it disappears when the session ends. So how should our retailer choose? The cleaned orders table is permanent, because the business depends on it. A batch table that is rebuilt from files every night can be transient, because the files are its backup, and it avoids paying for Fail-safe storage. Remember that all retained history is billed storage, so keep what recovery truly needs, and no more.

Reloading one day of orders should be a single unit of work. Delete the day's rows, insert the corrected ones, and log the reload, so that either everything happens or nothing does. With autocommit on, which is the default, every statement is its own transaction. To group statements, you begin a transaction explicitly and finish it with commit or rollback. Now look at the script on the left. It begins a transaction, deletes and inserts, and then creates a log table. That create statement is data definition language, D D L, and in Snowflake any D D L statement first commits whatever transaction is open. So the delete and the insert are committed right there. The create runs as its own transaction. The log insert that follows runs in autocommit and commits on its own too. When the script reaches rollback, there is nothing left to roll back. What looked like one unit was actually three separate commits, and a failure halfway through would have left the day half reloaded. The fix is simple once you know the rule. Keep explicit transactions to data changes and queries, and create any tables before you begin. And remember that other sessions see a transaction's changes only once it commits, never part way through. Two smaller rules complete the picture: changing the autocommit setting itself triggers a commit, and if a client disconnects with a transaction still open, that transaction is rolled back.

Merge is how most incremental loads apply changes. It matches source rows to target rows on a key, updates the ones that match, and inserts the ones that don't. But merge is only well defined when each target row matches at most one source row. Today's customer updates contain two rows for customer C two oh seven, who moved to Leeds in the morning and to York before lunch. Both rows match the same target row. Which city should win? By default, Snowflake refuses to guess, and the merge fails with a duplicate row error. There is a parameter that turns this check off, and then Snowflake picks one of the duplicates, with no promise about which. That is a silent, random data error, so don't reach for it. The real fix is to give merge exactly one source row per key. Here, qualify with row number, partitioned by customer and ordered by the update time, newest first, keeps only the latest change for each customer. One more detail: if two updates could share the same timestamp, the ordering itself is ambiguous, so add a tie-breaker, such as a sequence number from the source. And because merge is a single statement, its updates and inserts apply together or not at all. Then check the outcome. C two oh seven now lives in York. C three eight eight is new, so it is inserted. And C one fifty, with no update, is untouched.

Time Travel lets you read a table as it was in the past, as long as the moment is still within the table's retention period. You can ask for a timestamp, an offset such as twenty minutes ago, or, most precisely, the moment just before a particular statement ran. Here is why that matters. At five past two, someone ran an update on orders and forgot the where clause. Every order became cancelled, and by twenty past two, the revenue dashboard showed zero. The first step is to look, not to act. Querying the table before that update's statement ID shows the state we want back: four shipped, one pending, one cancelled. The second step is the repair. Clone the table as it was before the statement, then swap the clone into place, which exchanges the two tables in one operation. One caution: any legitimate changes written after the bad statement are not in the clone, so they have to be applied again. Time Travel also powers undrop. A table dropped by mistake can be restored within its retention period. If a new table with the same name was created in the meantime, rename that one first. Hybrid tables don't support undrop. And once retention has passed, only Fail-safe remains, which Snowflake performs for you on request. It is never a self-service query.

A clone is one of Snowflake's most useful tricks. When you clone a database, a schema or a table, the new object simply points at the same micro-partitions as the source. Nothing is copied, so even a large database clones in seconds, and at first the clone costs no extra storage. That makes it ideal for a test environment: our team clones the retail database into retail dev and experiments freely. From that moment, the two are independent. When production loads new orders, it writes new micro-partitions that belong only to production, and the clone never sees them. When a tester updates rows in the clone, the changed data goes into new micro-partitions that belong only to the clone. The unchanged partitions stay shared. Storage therefore grows only with changed data, and it is billed to the table that first wrote it. Two cautions. First, a clone is not a backup. It lives in the same account, in the same Region, under the same administrators, so whatever could destroy the source could destroy the clone too. Second, cloning a table does not copy its grants unless you ask for copy grants. And if you delete data from the source that a clone still uses, those bytes stay stored, and stay billed, for as long as the clone needs them.

Everything in this chapter so far has been about standard tables, and for analytics they remain the default. Snowflake also offers other table types, and the honest way to compare them is by their boundaries: where the data lives, and what Snowflake can promise about it. Iceberg tables store data as Apache Iceberg files, an open format that other engines such as Spark can read too. With Snowflake acting as the catalog, you get full data changes from Snowflake. If the files live in your own cloud storage, though, protecting and recovering them is your responsibility, not Fail-safe's. External tables let you query files sitting in a stage without loading them at all, which is handy for occasional reads of an archive, but they are read-only. Hybrid tables store rows rather than columns, for fast single-row reads and writes at high concurrency. They require a primary key and enforce it, unlike standard tables, but they don't support undrop. For our retailer, the core stays standard. A shared lake for the data science team might use Iceberg, old files might stay external, and an order-status lookup for the app might suit a hybrid table. Always start from the requirement, and check edition, Region and current limits before committing. With tables understood, the next chapter loads real data into them.

Data rarely arrives as rows. It arrives as files, and before Snowflake can load a file, the file has to wait somewhere Snowflake can read it. That place is a stage. There are four kinds. Every user has a personal stage, and every table has a stage of its own; both exist automatically and suit small, one-off loads. A named internal stage keeps files in Snowflake's own storage and can be shared with whichever roles you grant. And a named external stage points at your own cloud storage, through the storage integration we built in chapter two. That last kind is our retailer's landing path. The order system drops one CSV file a day into the landing bucket, and the landing stage in the raw schema reads it. Before loading anything, list the stage. It shows exactly which files are waiting, their sizes, and when they changed. Here there are two: the daily file, and a second one called orders resend that arrived a few hours later. Hold on to that second file; it matters in section four. Finally, a stage holds files, but it does not say how to read them. That is the job of a file format: the delimiter, whether there is a header, how dates are written, and which values mean null. Defining it once, as a named object, keeps every load reading the same file in the same way.

With files staged, copy into loads them, using a warehouse you choose. The simplest form copies each file column into the table column in the same position, but that silently assumes the file and the table agree forever. The safer pattern names everything. Inside copy, a select over the stage refers to file fields by position, dollar one, dollar two and so on, and the column list says exactly which table column each one fills. That is also where conversions become visible. Our source writes dates as day, month, year, so the file format's date setting tells Snowflake how to read them. Status arrives in lower case, so upper normalises it at the door, before inconsistent casing spreads into every report. And the total arrives as text, which the table's numeric type converts to an exact two-decimal amount. Notice the last two columns. Every file row also carries metadata: the name of the file it came from, and its row number within that file. Storing them costs almost nothing, and when someone questions a value months later, you can trace it straight back to its file and line. Why go to this trouble rather than rely on column order? Because a source that one day swaps two columns would otherwise load wrong values without a single error. One practical note: validation mode can't test a copy that transforms data, so validate a plain load of the same files first.

Sooner or later a file contains a row that cannot load. The questions are when you find out, and what happens to the rest of the file. To find out early, copy can run as a dry run. With validation mode set to return errors, it tests the staged files and loads nothing at all. Here it reports one problem: line five of the third of October file has a total of N A, which is not a number. Next, decide what a real load should do with that row. The on error option makes the choice. Abort statement is the default for copy: a single bad row stops the whole load, which is safe but means one typo can hold up a day's data. Skip file is the default for Snowpipe, which we meet shortly: the entire file containing the bad row is left unloaded. Continue loads every good row and reports the bad ones. Whichever you choose, the rule is the same: never lose a rejected row. After a continue load, the validate function returns that job's rejected records, and storing them in a quarantine table means they are counted, owned, and fixed at the source rather than forgotten. And remember that a skipped file is a rejection too. If nobody is watching for it, a whole day of orders can quietly go missing.

So what happens if a load runs twice? Copy keeps load metadata for each table, a record of which files it has loaded, for sixty-four days. When the same copy runs again over the same folder, files it has already loaded are skipped. Here is the second of October. At six, copy loads the daily file: six rows. At half past six, a scheduler retries the job after a timeout. The file is recognised and skipped, and nothing is duplicated. So far, so safe. Then at nine, the source system resends three orders it believes went missing, in a new file called orders resend. To the load metadata, that is a new file, so copy loads it: three more rows. Orders one thousand and one to one thousand and three now appear twice in raw orders. This is exactly where the nine rows we met in chapter two came from. The boundary is the important lesson. Load metadata protects against loading the same file twice. It knows nothing about orders, so it cannot protect against the same orders arriving in a different file. Force set to true deliberately reloads files, duplicates and all. And Snowpipe keeps its own separate metadata, so mixing both on one table can double-load. The control that actually works is deduplicating on the business key, the order ID, downstream, and testing that it holds.

A daily copy is fine for a daily file, but the customer app wants order status within minutes. Snowpipe closes that gap. A pipe is simply a copy statement wrapped in an object. With auto ingest turned on, your cloud storage sends an event notification whenever a new file lands, Snowflake queues it, and the pipe loads that file on serverless compute that Snowflake supplies. There is no warehouse to size or schedule. Under Snowflake's current simplified pricing, Snowpipe is billed per gigabyte ingested, at a published rate of zero point zero zero three seven credits per gigabyte, so check the current rate for your account. A few behaviours differ from bulk copy. A pipe keeps its own load metadata for fourteen days rather than sixty-four. And its default on error behaviour is to skip a file containing errors, rather than abort. Because Snowpipe runs on its own, you need evidence that it is working. The pipe status function shows how many files are pending and whether the pipe is running. Copy history shows every file it loaded, with row counts and errors. And pipe usage history shows the credits and bytes billed. Watch for the quiet failures in particular. A missed notification, a skipped file, or a paused pipe raises no alarm by itself, so somebody has to be looking.

Snowpipe still works in files. When the source is a stream of events, from an application or a Kafka topic, writing files first only adds delay. Snowpipe Streaming removes that step. A client, using Snowflake's ingest SDK, writes rows directly, and they become queryable within seconds. The client writes through channels. In the current high-performance architecture, each channel is opened against a pipe object, which defines the target table and any transformation. Every batch the client sends carries an offset token, a position the client chooses, such as a Kafka offset. Snowflake records the last offset it has committed for each channel. That record is what makes recovery correct. Suppose the client crashes. Channel zero had sent up to five thousand one hundred and twenty, but only five thousand one hundred was committed. On restart, the client asks for the last committed offset and resumes from the next one, so nothing is lost and nothing is written twice. Resuming from the last sent offset would silently drop twenty events. There are two architectures. The high-performance one uses the pipe object and is billed per uncompressed gigabyte. The classic one opens channels on tables directly; it is supported, but Snowflake plans to deprecate it. The choice of path follows the data: scheduled files suit copy, files as they land suit Snowpipe, and event rows suit streaming.

Sources change shape, usually without warning. Snowflake can absorb some of that automatically. Turn on schema evolution for a table, load with match by column name, and give the loading role the evolve schema privilege. Then a copy or Snowpipe load that finds a new column in the file adds it to the table, and a column missing from the file has its not null constraint dropped so the load can continue. In October, our source made three changes. First, it added a sales channel column. Schema evolution adds it, and that is genuinely safe. Second, it renamed order total to total amount. Evolution has no idea this is a rename. It adds a brand new total amount column and, because order total is now missing, drops its not null constraint. Every new order loads with a null order total, and revenue quietly falls. That is the dangerous one: it looks like success. Third, it started writing totals with a currency suffix. That cannot convert to a number, so the load rejects it loudly, which is actually the easier failure to deal with. Evolution won't change a column's type, won't recognise renames, and only applies to file and streaming loads, not to inserts or tasks. So treat the schema as a contract: watch the evolution records, test for sudden nulls, and agree changes with the source owner before they ship.

A load that succeeds proves only that bytes moved. It does not prove the right data arrived. Reconciliation is how you prove that, and it belongs inside ingestion, not after it. Our source sends a small manifest with each delivery: six orders, worth four hundred and ten pounds thirty-nine in total. We compare that against every hop. Raw orders holds nine rows but only six distinct orders, and its total is higher. That is not a mystery, because we know exactly why: the three resent orders. A difference you can explain is fine; a difference you cannot explain is an incident. The cleaned sales table holds six orders worth four hundred and ten thirty-nine, which matches the manifest exactly. Only then do we hand data on. Unloading uses the same copy command in the other direction: copy into a stage, from a query, writing Parquet files. Snowflake aims for files of about sixteen megabytes each by default, so expect several files unless you ask for a single one. It also does not warn you if the target path already contains files, so always write to a fresh, dated path. And a clean handoff is more than files. Send a manifest of row counts and totals, so the consumer can reconcile in turn, and the contract that says what each column means. That completes the loading chapter: next, we transform these rows into analytical products.

Every table has a grain: the thing that one row represents. Our orders table has one row per order. A new table, order lines, has one row per item on an order. Before writing any transformation, it pays to say the grain out loud, because joins change it. When you join orders to order lines, each order row is repeated once for every line it has. Order one thousand and one has two lines, so it appears twice. Order one thousand and three has three lines, so it appears three times. That is exactly what a join should do. The trouble starts when you then sum a column that belongs to the coarser grain. Summing the order total after the join counts each order once per line, and shipped revenue comes out at four hundred and fifty-one seventy. The real figure, from chapter one, is two hundred and twelve forty. Nothing failed. The query simply answered a different question. The fix is to keep each measure at its own grain. Here, summing the line amounts at the line grain gives the right answer. Alternatively, aggregate the lines up to one row per order before joining. A cheap habit catches this early: after any join, compare the row count with the count of distinct keys you expected.

Many analytical questions are about a row in relation to its neighbours. What is each customer's latest order? What share of their spending was this order? Window functions answer these without collapsing rows. A group by returns one row per group. A window function returns every input row, with extra columns computed across a related set of rows, called the partition. Here, row number ranks each customer's orders by date, newest first. A windowed sum puts each customer's total on every one of their rows, so C two oh seven's two orders both show one hundred and sixty-four forty. Then qualify filters on the window result, in the same way that having filters on aggregates, and keeps only rank one: one latest order per customer. Look closely at C two oh seven, though. Both orders were placed on the same date. Ordering by date alone leaves a tie, and Snowflake is free to break it differently each time the query runs, so the latest order could flip between runs. Adding the order ID as a second sort key makes the result deterministic: order one thousand and three. This is the same tie-breaker rule we met with merge in chapter three. Finally, the with clause, a common table expression, gives each step a name, which keeps a long transformation readable and reviewable.

The order events we streamed in chapter four arrive as JSON, stored in a single VARIANT column called payload. VARIANT holds semi-structured data as it arrived, and current releases allow a value of up to a hundred and twenty-eight megabytes. To read inside it, you use a path. Payload colon order ID reads a top-level key. Payload colon customer dot ID walks into a nested object. Each result is still a VARIANT, so cast it, with double colon, to the type you actually want. One trap: keys are case-sensitive. Ask for Order underscore Id with capitals and you get null, with no error at all. Arrays need FLATTEN. Event one thousand and seven has two items. Lateral flatten over the items array produces one row per item, so that single event becomes two rows, each with its own SKU and line amount. Event one thousand and eight has an empty items array, perhaps an order that was cancelled immediately. By default, flatten produces no rows for an empty array, and that event silently disappears from the result. Setting outer to true keeps it, with nulls for the item columns. And remember section one: after flattening, the grain is one row per item, so summing an event-level field across those rows would amplify it in exactly the same way.

Two kinds of conversion cause more wrong reports than almost anything else: time zones and number types. Start with time. Our events are stored in UTC, in a timestamp without a time zone. An order placed at half past midnight in London on the second of October happened at half past eleven on the first, in UTC, because London is one hour ahead during summer time. Take the date of the stored value and that order lands on the first. The business, though, counts it on the second. The fix is to convert to the business's time zone first, then take the date. Defaults make this worse if you don't override them. A plain timestamp column means timestamp without time zone unless someone has changed the mapping. And the session time zone, which drives local timestamp types and functions such as current timestamp, defaults to Los Angeles. A London retailer who never sets it will see times eight hours out. So set the account's time zone deliberately, and name time zones explicitly in every conversion. Numbers have a similar trap. Float is a binary approximation, so point one plus point two is not exactly point three, and an equality test fails. Number with a fixed scale is exact decimal arithmetic. Every money column belongs in an exact number type. And note that division adds decimal places: ten divided by three returns three point three three three three three three, not three.

Once a transformation is right, consumers need a stable way to read it. A view is the simplest: it stores a query, not data, and runs that query whenever someone reads it. Daily revenue is a view over orders, and it is where the business definition of revenue lives: everything except cancelled orders, summed by date and store. Every dashboard that reads the view gets the same definition, and changing the definition happens in one place. Check its output against what we know. Store S zero one on the first of October shows two hundred and twelve forty, the shipped total from chapter one. Store S zero two shows fifty-eight, because the cancelled order is excluded. A secure view adds protection for a specific disclosure concern. Its definition is hidden from everyone except its owner, and Snowflake switches off certain optimizations that could otherwise reveal rows the view filters out. That protection costs performance, so use secure views where disclosure matters, such as the partner view of one store, not everywhere. And a secure view protects one interface; it is not a replacement for the masking and row access policies we meet in chapter nine. A materialized view goes further and stores precomputed results, which Snowflake keeps current in the background. It can read only one table, with no joins, needs Enterprise edition, and costs storage plus maintenance compute.

So far we have transformed tables one query at a time. A dimensional model organises them for analysis. At the centre is a fact table, which records business events at one declared grain. Ours is one row per order line, with measures such as quantity and amount. Around it sit dimensions: date, product, store and customer, which describe the who, what, where and when of each fact. The interesting part is history. In chapter three, our merge overwrote customer C two oh seven's city: Hull became York, and Hull was gone. That is fine for a mailing list, but it changes the past. If finance asks for October revenue by city, should C two oh seven's orders from the first of October count in Hull, where the customer lived when they ordered, or York, where they live now? A type two dimension keeps both. Each change adds a new row with the dates it was valid from and to, and a flag for the current one. Facts join to whichever row was valid when the event happened. Now there are two honest answers: revenue by city as it was, which puts the orders in Hull, and as it is, which puts them in York. Neither is wrong, but the question must say which it means. The same goes for the definition of revenue itself: write it down, version it, and date its changes.

Not every transformation is written in SQL. Snowpark lets Python developers build the same transformations as DataFrames. The key idea is that a Snowpark DataFrame is lazy. Reading the orders table gives you a reference, not data. Each filter, group by and aggregate adds a step to a plan held on the client. Nothing has run yet. Only an action turns the plan into SQL, sends it to Snowflake, and runs it on a warehouse. That is pushdown: the computation happens where the data lives, exactly as if you had written the SQL yourself. Which action you call decides how much data travels. Save as table runs the query and writes the result inside Snowflake, so no rows leave at all. Count runs the query and returns a single number. Collect returns every result row to the client, which is fine for a small aggregate. To pandas returns every row too, into the client's memory, and called on a whole table, it drags all of it across the network into one machine. The boundary to respect is simple. Let Snowflake reduce the data first, with filters and aggregates, and only then bring a small result back. Pulling a large table into Python to aggregate it there defeats the point of the platform. When you genuinely need many rows locally, to pandas batches streams them in chunks rather than all at once.

The last tools in this chapter package logic so it can be reused. A user-defined function computes a value, and it can be used anywhere an expression can, inside a select or a where clause. Net amount is one: it returns zero for cancelled orders and the total otherwise. What a UDF cannot do is change data; it runs queries only. A stored procedure is the opposite. You call it, it runs a sequence of steps, including inserts, deletes and even D D L, and it returns a single value to the caller, not a value per row. Reload day is a procedure. It wraps chapter three's delete and insert in one explicit transaction, written correctly this time, with no D D L in the middle. Procedures raise a question functions don't: whose privileges do they use? By default, a procedure runs with owner's rights, meaning the privileges of the role that owns it, here retail admin. That lets us grant the analyst role permission to call reload day without ever granting it delete on orders: a narrow, fixed capability. A caller's rights procedure runs with the caller's own privileges and can see their session. Owner's rights is powerful, so never build SQL from a caller's input inside one. These building blocks are what chapter seven automates into pipelines.

In chapter three we merged a daily extract of customer updates. Now the CRM sends something richer: a change feed. Every insert, update and delete in the CRM is captured, in order, and delivered to Snowflake. It is worth being precise here, because two quite different things both get called changes. The first is source change data capture. A CDC tool reads the CRM's own transaction log and lands every event as a row in raw customer changes. On the second of October there were four: customer C two oh seven moved to Leeds, C three eight eight signed up in Bath, C two oh seven moved again to York, and C three one one was deleted. Each event carries the source's sequence number and the time it happened. This table is the history of our customers, so we keep it. The second is a Snowflake stream. A stream tracks changes to one Snowflake table since a bookmark called its offset. It stores no data of its own; it reads the table's versions, and only as far back as the table's retention allows. And it returns the net change, not every intermediate step. The rule for this chapter follows directly: land the source's events durably, and use streams only to find out what is new since the last time you looked.

A stream feels like a queue of changes, but it isn't one. What a stream actually stores is a single bookmark, called its offset: a point in the version history of the table it watches. When you read the stream, Snowflake compares the table at the offset with the table now, and returns the difference. Our stream was last consumed at eight in the morning. Since then, four events have landed in the change log, so reading the stream now returns events one oh one to one oh four. A cheap function, stream has data, tells you whether there is anything to process before you spend compute on it. Because a stream reads the table's own versions, it costs almost no storage. But that is also its limit. Old versions exist only within the table's data retention period. If a stream goes unread for longer than that, Snowflake will hold the history for it a little longer, up to the max data extension setting, which defaults to fourteen days. Beyond that point, shown as stale after in show streams, the stream becomes stale. A stale stream can no longer be read at all; it has to be recreated, and the changes it missed must be recovered some other way. So watch the stale after timestamp, and alert well before it, not when the first read fails.

There is an important difference between reading a stream and consuming it. Reading is just a select: you see the changes, and nothing else happens. Consuming means using the stream inside a data-changing statement, such as an insert or a merge, and the offset only advances when that statement's transaction commits. Watch three attempts at ten past twelve. First, someone selects from the stream to see what is waiting. Four rows come back, and the offset doesn't move. Second, the merge into customers runs, but fails halfway, perhaps the warehouse was suspended. The transaction rolls back, and because nothing committed, the offset doesn't move either. The same four rows are still waiting. Third, the merge runs again and commits. Only now does the offset advance, to five past twelve. Note that wrapping a plain select in an explicit transaction changes nothing; only a data-changing statement moves the offset. This behaviour is exactly what you want. A failed run loses nothing and skips nothing, so recovery is simply running it again. If two statements need the same changes, such as a merge and an audit insert, wrap them in one explicit transaction, and both see an identical change set. But notice what consuming means for anyone else: once committed, those changes are gone from that stream. A second consumer must have a stream of its own, with its own offset.

What does a stream actually return? Each row comes with extra metadata columns. Metadata action says whether the row is an insert or a delete, and metadata is update says whether it is part of an update. That is because a stream has no separate update action. An update appears as a pair of rows: the old version as a delete, and the new version as an insert, both flagged as part of an update. Here is a standard stream on the customers table, covering the second of October. Customer C two oh seven shows a delete of Hull and an insert of York, both marked as an update. C three eight eight is a plain insert, and C three one one is a plain delete. Now look for Leeds. It isn't there. C two oh seven really did live in Leeds for a couple of hours, but a stream returns only the net difference between its offset and now, so intermediate states vanish. Streams come in two modes. A standard stream returns inserts, updates and deletes, which requires work to pair old and new rows. An append-only stream returns inserted rows only, and is cheaper to read. Our raw change log is insert-only, so an append-only stream suits it perfectly. The lesson is the same as section one: if you need every intermediate step, read the source log.

Now we can apply the changes. An incremental merge reads only what is new in the stream, and matches it to the customers table on the business key, the customer ID. Four rules make it correct, and all four live in one statement. First, one event per key. The stream may hold several events for the same customer, so qualify keeps only the one with the highest source sequence. That is chapter three's lesson again: merge needs one source row per target row. Second, deletes. An event with operation D removes the customer. Third, never go backwards. The update only happens when the incoming sequence is higher than the one already stored on the row. Fourth, new keys are inserted, unless their latest event is a delete, in which case there is nothing to insert. Check the outcome. C two oh seven moves to York, with sequence one oh three. C three eight eight is inserted. C three one one is removed. C one fifty is untouched. Now run exactly the same batch again. Every incoming sequence is equal to the stored one, so nothing changes. The merge is idempotent, which means re-runs are always safe. Notice what made that possible: storing the source sequence on every target row. Without it, the guard has nothing to compare against.

Change feeds don't always arrive in order. Network delays, retries and parallel extraction mean an older event can land after a newer one. Here, event one oh one, C two oh seven's move to Leeds at nine o'clock, was delayed. Event one oh three, the move to York at half past eleven, landed first, and Leeds arrived ten minutes later. Now it matters which rule decides. If the last event loaded wins, C two oh seven ends up in Leeds: an older change has silently overwritten a newer one. If the highest source sequence wins, York stays, which is correct. That is exactly what our guarded merge does. Ordering by the time the change happened can also work, but only if every source system's clock agrees, so a sequence from the source log is safer. Deletes need the same care. A delete event is called a tombstone, and it must be applied, not skipped. You can remove the row, or keep it with an is deleted flag, which preserves history and keeps old orders linked to a real customer. And a late update that arrives after a tombstone must not bring the customer back to life. Finally, when you build history, such as chapter five's type two dimension, date each version by when the change happened in the business, never by when it happened to load.

Incremental pipelines are efficient, but they will eventually go wrong, and the right recovery depends on what was lost and what you still have. Take the easy case first. A single run failed. Because the offset never moved, you simply run it again, and the same changes are applied. Now a harder one. The stream went unread for too long and became stale. It cannot be read, so recreate it, which starts a fresh offset from now. But the changes it missed are gone from the stream's point of view. The answer is to rebuild the customers table from the full event log: take the latest event for each customer, drop those whose latest event is a delete, and you have the current state, independent of any stream. Suppose instead the merge logic itself was wrong for a week. Replay that week's events, or the whole log, into a rebuilt table, compare it with the live one, and swap it in once the counts and a sample agree. And if a source resends old events, nothing is needed at all: the sequence guard ignores them. Every hard case relies on the same thing. A stream is a cursor; it cannot replay the past. The landed event log is the archive that makes rebuilds possible, so keep it. Next, chapter seven automates this whole loop.

Everything we have built so far ran because someone ran it. This chapter makes it run by itself. The basic unit is a task. A task holds exactly one SQL statement, or one call to a procedure, plus two decisions: when it runs, and what compute it runs on. Our retailer has two. The nightly load runs on a schedule, a CRON expression for half past five every morning, London time, and uses the load warehouse. The customer apply task has no schedule at all. It is triggered: its when clause checks whether chapter six's stream has data, and it runs only when there are changes to apply. It uses serverless compute, which Snowflake sizes for you, up to the equivalent of a two X large warehouse. A warehouse task, by contrast, runs on a warehouse you size and pay for by the second. Two things surprise people. First, every task is created suspended, so nothing happens until you resume it. Second, a task needs permission to run at all. The role that owns it must hold the execute task privilege, which only an account administrator can grant, plus usage on its warehouse, or execute managed task for serverless. And the task runs with its owner role's privileges, so that role must be able to do everything the SQL inside it does.

Real pipelines have steps that depend on each other, so tasks connect into a graph. Each child task names its predecessor with after, and only the root task carries the schedule. Our nightly graph starts with load orders, which copies the new file into raw. Clean orders follows, deduplicating raw into sales. Then two builds run in parallel, because neither needs the other: the order lines fact table and the customer dimension. Finally, finalize run is a special task called a finalizer. It runs after every other task has finished, and crucially, it runs even when something failed, which makes it the right place to log the outcome and clean up. Each task in the graph can choose its own compute, so a heavy build can use a bigger warehouse while a small step runs serverless. Then there is identity: who is the pipeline acting as? By default, a task runs as a system user carrying the privileges of the task's owner role. Snowflake also lets a task run as a named user, which makes its actions attributable in the logs. Notice one more rule. Every task in a graph has the same owner. That is a useful constraint: exactly one role answers for the whole pipeline, and its privileges define everything the pipeline can do.

Here is the night of the third of October. Load orders succeeded, and so did clean orders, which updated the sales orders table. Then build lines failed, while build customer succeeded, and the finalizer logged the run as failed. Look at the committed column. A task graph is not a transaction. Each task commits its own work, so when build lines failed, the change clean orders made to sales orders had already happened, and nothing rolled it back. For a few hours, sales is up to date but the fact table is stale. Recovery starts with retry. Execute task with retry last re-runs only the tasks that failed, rather than the whole graph. You can also ask Snowflake to retry automatically, with task auto retry attempts on the root task, but the default is zero, so it only happens if you set it. If a task keeps failing, after ten consecutive failures by default it suspends itself, so someone has to notice. Overlap matters too. With the default overlap policy, no overlap, a new scheduled run waits rather than running alongside one that is still going. This setting replaced an older parameter, allow overlapping execution. But the real safeguard isn't a parameter. Retries and reruns are only safe when each task is idempotent, like chapter six's guarded merge, so running it twice does no harm.

Tasks describe how to do the work, step by step. Dynamic tables take the opposite approach: you declare the result you want, and how fresh it must be, and Snowflake works out the rest. A dynamic table is defined by a query. Our pipeline has two. Orders clean deduplicates the raw orders, using the same qualify pattern as before. Revenue DT aggregates the cleaned orders into daily revenue by store. Snowflake reads the queries, sees that revenue DT depends on orders clean, and schedules refreshes in the right order without you writing a single after clause. The freshness requirement is called target lag. Revenue DT has a target lag of fifteen minutes, meaning its contents should never be more than fifteen minutes behind its sources. Orders clean uses downstream, which means it has no clock of its own and refreshes whenever revenue DT needs it. That is why at least one table in a chain must have a time-based lag. The minimum lag is one minute, and a table can't be fresher than the tables it reads. Be precise about what this promises. Target lag is a goal Snowflake schedules towards. Look at the refresh history: the twenty-four past nine refresh took nineteen minutes, so for a while the dashboard's data was twenty-two minutes old, missing the target. And every refresh runs on the warehouse you named, so freshness has a cost.

Every dynamic table refresh is either incremental, processing only the rows that changed since last time, or full, recomputing the whole result. Incremental is usually far cheaper, but it is only possible when Snowflake can work out how the query's output changes as its input changes. The refresh mode is set when you create the table. Auto lets Snowflake decide, and here is the subtle part: it decides once, at creation, and the choice is then fixed. If the query contains something incremental refresh can't handle, such as random, rollup or cube, except, or a recursive query, auto quietly resolves to full, and every refresh recomputes everything. The refresh mode reason column tells you why. If you set incremental explicitly, Snowflake refuses to create the table instead, which is why explicit modes are the safer choice in production: a surprise becomes an error, not a bill. Two more lifecycle details matter. Initialize on create fills the table during the create statement; on schedule leaves it empty, and unreadable, until the first scheduled refresh. And changes behave differently. Altering the target lag or the warehouse keeps the existing data. But create or replace always reinitializes the table, recomputing it from scratch, even if the definition didn't change.

We now have three ways to keep a result current, and none of them is always right. The question is what the logic needs. A dynamic table is declarative. You state the result as a query, joins and aggregates included, and Snowflake manages dependencies and refreshes against a freshness goal. What it can't do is anything procedural: no side effects, no calling procedures, no sending notifications, and any special apply rules have to be expressible as a query. Streams and tasks are the opposite. You write the change logic yourself, so you can do anything: sequence guards, tombstones, several steps in a specific order. That control costs more code, and making every step safe to re-run is your job. Materialized views sit to one side: one table, no joins, kept current by Snowflake on serverless compute, best for a hot aggregate over a single large table. So here is how our retailer chooses. Daily revenue is a pure aggregate with a freshness requirement, which is exactly what a dynamic table expresses. Customers come from a change feed with out-of-order events and deletes, so the guarded merge from chapter six, run by a stream-triggered task, is the better fit. In fairness, that particular rule, latest event wins and tombstones drop out, can also be written as a query, so it could be a dynamic table too; the merge earns its place when the apply logic grows beyond what one query can say. And the day reload has steps and side effects, so a task calls a procedure. Choose by the logic, not the feature.

A pipeline can succeed every night and still deliver wrong data. A task's status only proves that it ran. To know the output is right, you need evidence about the data itself. Snowflake's data metric functions provide that. You attach them to a table and they run on a schedule. Here we attach three to sales orders: duplicate count on the order ID, which should always be zero after deduplication; null count on the total; and freshness on the updated timestamp, which reports how many seconds old the newest row is. Each scheduled measurement lands in a results view. Data metric functions are an Enterprise edition feature, and scheduled measurements run on serverless compute that is billed, so measure what matters, not everything. Measurements only help if someone acts on them, so an alert closes the loop. An alert checks a condition on a schedule and, when it is true, does something, here sending an email if orders are more than an hour stale. Put together, a well-run pipeline has three kinds of evidence. Task history shows what ran, when, and whether it failed. Dynamic table refresh history shows the actual lag achieved, not just the target. And the quality results show what the data actually looks like. You need all three to say the pipeline worked.

Not every team schedules inside Snowflake. Many already use an orchestrator such as Airflow to coordinate work across systems, and dbt to define their models and tests. Both work well with Snowflake, as long as the responsibilities are clear. The orchestrator owns scheduling and the dependencies that cross system boundaries, such as waiting for a source system's export before loading. When it connects to Snowflake, it does so as a service user, our loader service user from chapter two, authenticating with a key pair rather than a password. Everything that happens inside Snowflake still follows Snowflake's rules: the warehouse provides compute, statements commit as transactions, and the service user's roles decide what it may touch. dbt can also run inside Snowflake itself. With dbt Projects on Snowflake, the project is stored as a Snowflake object, and execute dbt project runs it, with either a Snowflake task or the external orchestrator deciding when. That flexibility brings the one rule this section is really about. Every schedule needs exactly one owner. If both a Snowflake task and an Airflow DAG run the same dbt build, it will run twice, overlap, or fail in confusing ways, exactly as it did on the fourth of October, when two builds started at six, fought over the same models, and one of them failed. Decide who owns each schedule, write it down, and the evidence from both sides will tell one consistent story.

Our retail product has grown. A history table now holds three years of orders, about one point two billion rows, and one dashboard query takes fourteen seconds. The temptation is to make the warehouse bigger. The discipline is to find out where the time actually went first. Query history is the starting point. It splits a query's total time into compilation, time spent queued, and execution. Here, queuing was zero, so the warehouse was free when the query arrived. The problem isn't waiting; it is the work itself. The query profile then shows that work as a tree of operators, each with its share of execution time. Read it from the bottom. The table scan took eighty-nine percent of the time. Its statistics say it scanned eighteen thousand two hundred and forty partitions, out of eighteen thousand two hundred and forty in total: it skipped nothing. Then look at the row counts on the edges. One point two billion rows came out of the scan, and only one point one million survived the filter. So almost everything read was thrown away straight afterwards. The aggregate and the join barely register. That gives us the habit for this whole chapter: find the dominant operator, explain it, fix it, and only then look at anything else.

So why did the scan read everything? To answer that, recall chapter one: Snowflake stores tables as micro-partitions, and for each one it records metadata, including the minimum and maximum value of every column. When a query filters on a column, Snowflake compares the filter with those ranges, and skips any partition that cannot possibly contain a match. That is called pruning, and it happens before any data is read. Now look at the slow query's filter. It turned the order date into text, year and month, and compared that with the string twenty twenty-six dash ten. The partition metadata holds dates, not that text, so Snowflake cannot use it, and every partition has to be read and tested. Rewrite the filter as a plain range on the date column itself, from the first of October up to, but not including, the first of November, and the metadata answers it directly. Only three hundred and twelve partitions can contain October dates, so only those are read. The result is identical, and the query drops from fourteen seconds to about one, without a single extra credit of compute. Pruning works best when you compare the column itself, when data arrives roughly in date order, so each partition covers a narrow range, and when you select only the columns you need.

Before claiming that a rewrite made a query faster, you have to be sure what you measured. Run the pruned query three times and you get three very different numbers. The first run, on a freshly resumed warehouse, takes one point one seconds and reads about one and a half gigabytes from remote storage. The second run, with exactly the same text, takes less than a tenth of a second and scans nothing at all. That is the result cache. When an identical query runs against data that hasn't changed, Snowflake returns the stored result without using a warehouse. Results are kept for twenty-four hours, and each reuse extends that, up to thirty-one days from the first run. The third run turns result reuse off for the session. It scans the same bytes, but takes only point six of a second, because the data is still on the warehouse's local disk from the first run. That warehouse cache belongs to one warehouse only, and it disappears when the warehouse suspends, so an aggressive auto-suspend trades cache warmth for credits. So, to compare two versions of a query fairly, disable result reuse, run each several times on the same warehouse, compare the warm medians, and record bytes and partitions scanned, which don't depend on caching at all. One exception to remember: queries on hybrid tables never use the result cache.

Two very different problems both get reported as the warehouse is slow, and they need opposite remedies. The first is one query that is slow on its own. Its profile shows long execution, perhaps spilling to disk, and no time spent queued. Here a bigger warehouse can help, because each size step doubles the compute, and also doubles the credits per hour, from one for extra small, through two, four, eight, to sixteen for extra large on first-generation standard warehouses. Second-generation standard warehouses, generally available since twenty twenty-five, run on faster hardware at different rates, so check which your account uses. That is scaling up. The second is the nine o'clock rush: forty people open their dashboards at once. Each query is quick, but they queue behind one another, and query history shows the time as queued overload. A bigger warehouse is the wrong tool here. What helps is more warehouses of the same size, which is what a multi-cluster warehouse does. Set a minimum of one cluster and a maximum of three, and Snowflake starts extra clusters while queries are queuing, then shuts them down. Forty-five minutes at three small clusters costs four and a half credits. Multi-cluster needs Enterprise edition, and the standard scaling policy favours avoiding queues, while economy favours saving credits. And before either, isolate workloads. Our dashboards and loads already have their own warehouses, so a heavy load can never queue a dashboard.

Once the scan is fixed, other shapes of slowness show up in the profile, and each has its own first fix. The first is spill. When an operation such as a big sort or join produces more intermediate data than fits in the warehouse's memory, it spills to the warehouse's local disk, which is slower, and if even that runs out, to remote cloud storage, which is much slower still. The profile reports both amounts. The first fix is to reduce how many rows reach that operator. If it still spills after that, a larger warehouse has more memory, and that is a legitimate reason to scale up. The second is skew. Snowflake spreads work across many workers, but if one key value, say one enormous customer, owns most of the rows, one worker does most of the work while the others wait. A bigger warehouse barely helps; handling that hot key separately does. The third is join shape. A join whose output is many times larger than its inputs is usually the grain problem from chapter five. And a filter that only runs after a large join wastes work: the rewrite on the right restricts orders to October first, then joins one month of lines instead of three years. The order of attack is always the same. Reshape the work first, and buy compute last.

Some workloads stay slow even after a good rewrite, and for those Snowflake offers ways to do work in advance, so that reads become cheaper. Each one runs serverless maintenance in the background, and you pay for it continuously, whether or not anyone queries. A clustering key asks Snowflake to keep a table's rows physically ordered by some columns, such as order date, so that range filters prune well even when data arrives out of order. Search optimization builds a structure that finds a handful of rows in a huge table, which is ideal for point lookups such as one order by its ID; it needs Enterprise edition and often adds storage of around a quarter of the table. A materialized view stores the result of a repeated aggregate over one table, again on Enterprise edition. The common thread is cost. Maintenance grows with how much the underlying table changes, so a table that is rewritten constantly can cost a lot to keep clustered or optimized. Snowflake is also changing how clustering is billed: newly clustered tables move to a model called Optima. So before enabling any of them, try a rewrite first, which is often enough and always free. Then estimate the cost with the system estimate functions, enable it, and watch its history views to confirm the estimate held.

By this point in the course, our product spends credits in many more places than the two warehouses we started with. Each line on the bill has a driver, the thing that makes it grow, and a view that shows it. Warehouses are billed for the hours they run multiplied by their size, and that includes dynamic table refreshes, which run on the warehouse you named. Serverless features are each metered separately: tasks, Snowpipe, automatic clustering, data quality measurements, each with its own history view. Cloud services, as we saw in chapter one, only appear on days they exceed ten percent of warehouse usage. Storage is billed separately, by average terabytes per month, and it includes more than live data. Time Travel and Fail-safe hold the old versions of changed rows, so a table that is rewritten every night can carry far more history than its own size. And moving data out to another Region or cloud is charged as data transfer. Now read the illustrative October ledger. Most of it is what you would expect. But look at automatic clustering: one hundred and eighty credits, more than the load warehouse, and nearly as much as dashboards. Nobody runs it; it simply happens in the background. Maintenance costs like that are exactly the ones that are easy to miss.

Knowing where credits go is half the job; the other half is keeping them under control, and here the coverage of each tool matters a great deal. A resource monitor watches warehouses. You give it a credit quota, and triggers that notify at, say, eighty percent and suspend the warehouse at one hundred. It also counts the cloud services that support those warehouses. But it is blind to serverless spend. Tasks on serverless compute, automatic clustering and Snowpipe never touch a resource monitor, so the one hundred and eighty credits of clustering from the last section would sail straight past it. Budgets fill that gap. An account budget covers everything, and a custom budget covers a chosen group of objects, including all of their serverless and background costs. A budget has a monthly limit in credits and notifies when spend is projected to exceed it. What it does not do is stop anything. It can call a procedure if you write one, and those actions can lag by hours. Attribution answers the question of whose spend it is: tag warehouses and tables with a cost centre, and group usage by tag. Finally, remember the latency. The account usage views run hours behind, so today's surprise usually appears tomorrow. Controls limit the damage; they do not replace someone looking.

Let's finish by judging an optimisation properly, because faster and cheaper are not the same thing. Good optimisation is a loop. Take a baseline with warm medians. Form one hypothesis about the cause. Make one change, ideally in a cloned development database. Compare on both time and credits. Then keep watching for regressions. Apply that to adding a clustering key on order date. Latency falls from fourteen point two seconds to one point one, which is a clear win. Partitions scanned drop from eighteen thousand to three hundred and twelve. Now the credits. The dashboard query runs about two hundred times a day, and the faster version saves roughly one and a half credits a day of dashboard compute. But keeping the history table clustered costs about six credits a day in background reclustering. Net, the system now costs about four times as much as before. So what should we do? Remember the predicate rewrite from section two. It reached the same one point one seconds for nothing. That comes first.
