Clustering is only justified if the business values that speed above about four and a half credits a day, perhaps for other queries that can't be rewritten. Whatever we decide, we write it down with the numbers, as a decision record. And we re-measure after the data grows, because today's win can be next quarter's regression.

This chapter is about keeping data safe and useful as more people and systems consume it. It starts with a plain question: what are we actually holding? You can't protect data you haven't found. Snowflake's classification inspects a table's columns and suggests two things for each: a semantic category, what kind of data it is, and a privacy category, how sensitive it is. On our customers table, email and full name come back as identifiers, data that points at one person on its own. Postcode, city and date of birth are quasi-identifiers: harmless alone, but together they can often re-identify someone. With auto-tagging on, the results are written as tags on the columns, and any value you set by hand is respected rather than overwritten. Tags carry more than sensitivity. A data owner tag names the team that decides who may use the data and how. Lineage then shows where a column goes. Email flows from the CRM change feed into customers, then into the customer dimension, and from there into a nightly export file, which is outside Snowflake altogether. Every hop is somewhere the protection has to hold. One limit is worth stating plainly. Classification, tags and lineage describe the data. None of them stops a single query. Enforcement is the next section.

Enforcement in Snowflake is done with policies, attached directly to tables and columns, so they apply however a query arrives: a dashboard, an export, a share, or someone typing SQL. Policies are an Enterprise edition feature. There are two main kinds. A row access policy decides which rows exist for the querying role. Ours lets analysts see every store, and lets a store manager see only customers whose home store is theirs, looked up in a small mapping table of role and store. A masking policy decides what a column shows. Ours keeps the email domain but hides the name, unless the session holds the support role. When both apply, the row policy runs first, and masking is applied to whatever rows remain. Now watch the same select under three roles. The analyst sees all three customers, with masked emails. The York manager sees only C one fifty, from store S zero two, also masked. Someone holding support alongside analyst sees all three, in the clear. Notice the policies use is role in session rather than current role, so they respect role hierarchy and secondary roles. Keeping the store rules in a mapping table means changing access is a data change, not a code change. Secure views from chapter five still help shape an interface, but policies protect the data itself, everywhere it is read.

Policies say who may read data. An auditor, or a privacy request, asks a different question: who actually did? Access history answers it. The access history view records, for every query, the base objects and the individual columns it read or wrote, and the policies that were applied while it ran. It keeps a year of history, and it is an Enterprise edition feature. Here we ask who read the email column of customers during October. The query flattens the list of objects and columns each query touched, keeps only those that read email, and joins to query history for the role. Three users appear. Ana, an analyst, read it forty-one times, and the masking policy applied every time, so she never saw a real address. The support bot read it in the clear, as its role allows. Whether twelve hundred reads in a month is expected is a question for the data owner, and this is exactly the evidence they need to answer it. The loader service user wrote the column, which is the normal ETL path. Be clear about what this evidence cannot prove. It shows what happened inside Snowflake. It cannot show what a user did with rows after an export left the platform. And like the other account usage views, it lags behind real time by a matter of hours, so it suits audit and review, not live alerting.

Sometimes the consumer isn't in your company at all. Our retailer's York store is run by a franchise partner, YorkCo, who has their own Snowflake account and needs daily revenue for their store. Rather than emailing files, RETAILCO shares it. A share lets another account query your objects live, with no copy made. Here is how it is built. We don't share the raw orders table. We share the partner revenue secure view from chapter five, which already restricts to store S zero two, and we grant it through a database role, partner read, which is granted to the share. On the other side, YorkCo creates a database from the share. It is read-only, and they grant the shared database role to whichever of their own roles should see it. Responsibilities divide cleanly. The provider pays for storage and owns correctness, freshness, and exactly which rows are exposed. The consumer pays for the compute to query it, using their own warehouse, and decides who in their organisation sees it. Masking and row policies travel with the data, but checks on the provider's role names don't mean anything in another account, so policies on shared data should test for database roles instead. One limit leads into the next section: a direct share only reaches accounts in the same Region.

A direct share only works within one Region. Our second franchise partner runs on Azure in West Europe, so we need another mechanism, and each option moves cost and control somewhere different. For a consumer in the same Region with a Snowflake account, a direct share is simplest and copies nothing. For a consumer in another Region or cloud, a listing with auto-fulfillment is the usual route. Snowflake keeps a refreshed copy of the data product in the consumer's Region, and the provider pays for the replication, the storage, and the data transfer, but only in Regions where consumers actually exist. You can achieve the same by replicating the database yourself and sharing from a replica, which gives more control and more work, and needs an organisation administrator to enable replication first. And for a consumer with no Snowflake account at all, a provider can create a reader account, owning it and paying for its compute as well as the storage. So the EU partner gets a private listing, fulfilled into West Europe. That raises three questions before anyone clicks publish. First, residency: is this data allowed to leave the United States at all? Second, freshness: the EU copy is refreshed on an interval, so it is not live. And third, cost: replication and transfer now appear on our bill. Distribution is a governance decision, not just a technical one.

By now, daily revenue has four consumers: the finance dashboards, the store app, which queries it through the SQL API, the York partner through the share, and the nightly export from chapter four. Each depends on what revenue means, not just on the column names. Then finance decides revenue should be net of refunds. A twenty pound refund on order one thousand and three means store S zero one's revenue for the first of October moves from two hundred and twelve forty to one hundred and ninety-two forty. If we simply change the view, every consumer's numbers shift at the same moment. The schema is identical, so nothing errors. The partner's invoice is suddenly different. The app shows different totals from last week's report. Nobody was told. The fix is to version the interface. Publish daily revenue v two with the new definition, and say what it means in its comment. Leave v one exactly as it is, while each consumer moves across deliberately, and retire v one only after giving notice. Behind that is a written contract for each data product: its grain, its definition, its freshness, which here is within fifteen minutes from chapter seven's dynamic table, and how much notice consumers get before anything changes. Contracts turn surprise changes into scheduled ones.

Policies are code, and like any code they need tests. The trap is testing them as yourself. An administrator who runs a query and sees sensible results has proved nothing about what an analyst or a store manager sees. Snowflake can simulate that directly. Execute using policy context runs a query as if the session had a different role, and returns exactly what that role would get. So we keep a matrix: every role, the rows it should see, and whether email should be masked. Analysts see all stores, masked. Each store manager sees only their store. Support sees emails in the clear. And public, which every user has, should see nothing at all, so that row of the matrix matters as much as the others. The whole matrix is re-run on every policy change. Before changing a policy, check its blast radius. Policy references lists every table and column it is attached to. Remember that views and shares inherit the change, so it reaches every consumer at once, including partners. Finally, some trade-offs should be decided deliberately rather than discovered. A policy that looks up a mapping table runs on every query, which costs time. And the right to write and attach policies should sit with a governance role, separate from the teams that own the data. Next, chapter ten takes all of this through releases and incidents.

Over nine chapters, our retailer has accumulated a lot of objects: tables, views, policies, streams, tasks, dynamic tables and shares. Every one of them is code, and this chapter is about changing that code safely, and recovering when things go wrong anyway. The first step is to keep every definition in version control, in one Git repository. Snowflake's DCM projects let you describe objects declaratively. A define statement states what a table or view should look like, its desired state, and Snowflake works out how to get there, running it as create or alter, which became generally available in July twenty twenty-six. A manifest file lists the targets, and holds the variables that differ between them: which account, which database, which warehouse size. Our retailer has three targets. Development and test both live in the DEV account, in separate databases, and production lives in PROD. The rule that keeps this honest is that environments differ only by configuration. Nobody hand-edits SQL in test or production, because a hand edit is a change nobody tested and nobody can reproduce. And what reaches production is exactly the commit that passed testing: one artefact, promoted, not rebuilt. With that in place, a release becomes a reviewable event instead of a series of console sessions.

Who actually runs a release matters as much as what it contains. If a release runs as whichever engineer happens to be on duty, objects end up owned by that person, grants get made by hand and forgotten, and nobody can say afterwards exactly what changed. So releases run as a dedicated identity: a deploy service user, of type service, authenticating with a key pair, exactly as chapter two recommended for workloads. Its role inherits retail admin, so everything it creates is owned by the same role that owns the rest of the retail database, not by a person. The pipeline runs a plan first, a human reviews the difference it will make, and only then does it deploy. Order matters too. Release one point four adds a refunds table and the new revenue view from chapter nine. Roles and grants must exist first, then tables, then the views that read them, then the pipelines that refresh them, and finally the shares that expose them to partners. Deploy a view before its table and it fails. Deploy a share before its view and the partner sees nothing. Declarative tools work out much of this ordering, but you still need to understand it to read a failure. And privilege changes are changes like any other. Grants belong in the release, reviewed in the same diff. A grant someone adds by hand in production is drift: the next declarative release either reverts it without warning or never knows it exists.

Testing data platforms has a reputation for being hard, but most of what matters can be checked with plain SQL, and each check reuses something from earlier in the course. Release one point four runs six checks in the test database before it can be promoted. First, the plan itself: it should add the refunds table and the new view, and drop nothing. An unexpected drop in a plan is the cheapest bug you'll ever catch. Second, a unit test on fixed input rows: with a twenty pound refund on order one thousand and three, store S zero one on the first of October must come out at one hundred and ninety-two forty. Third, a contract test. Version one of daily revenue must not move at all while consumers still read it, so we compare it before and after the release, and expect zero differing rows. Fourth, reconciliation against the source manifest, from chapter four. Fifth, the policy matrix from chapter nine, because a release that recreates a table can silently drop its policies. Sixth, a performance budget, so the new view stays under two seconds on the BI warehouse. Only then is the release promoted. After deploying, smoke-test both versions, watch the first task runs and refreshes, and write a release record: which commit, which checks passed, and who approved it. And when a check fails, nothing is promoted. Fix it in development and rerun the whole set, because a fix for one check can break another. A failing contract test is a special case: it means version one consumers would break, so the change belongs in a new version, as chapter nine showed, not in the existing one.

Here is what happened on the evening of the sixth of October, on an earlier attempt at release one point four. The release renamed a column on orders, from order total to gross total, and then tried to recreate daily revenue to use the new name. The second step failed on a syntax error. The rename had already committed, because, as we saw in chapter three, each D D L statement commits on its own, and there is no transaction wrapped around a whole release. So the table had changed, the view still referred to the old column name, and every dashboard showed an invalid identifier error. Reverting the Git commit didn't help at all. The repository went back to the old definition, but the renamed column in production didn't. Rolling back code is not the same as restoring data or schema. Two habits prevent this. The first is to change columns in stages. Expand: add the new column alongside the old one. Migrate: move readers across, one release at a time. Contract: drop the old column only once nothing reads it. At no point does a single failure leave readers broken. The second is to keep a way back. Cloning the database before a release takes seconds and copies nothing. But remember what a clone is: a restore point for state, so any rows loaded after it was taken must be re-applied.

At eight in the morning on the seventh of October, finance reports that today's dashboard still shows yesterday's revenue. Incidents like this are solved by walking backwards from the symptom, one layer at a time, checking evidence rather than guessing. The dashboard reads revenue DT. Its refresh history shows it refreshed successfully at five forty-one, so the dynamic table isn't broken; it faithfully reflected a source that hadn't changed. Its source is the cleaned orders, so next is the clean orders task. It never ran, because its predecessor in the task graph failed. That predecessor is load orders, and task history shows it failed at five thirty with an access denied error on the landing bucket. Now the timeline makes sense. At ten past ten the night before, someone edited the IAM role's trust policy in AWS, breaking the chain of permissions from chapter two. The fix itself took minutes: restore the trust policy and retry the failed task. But a good incident review also asks why it took two and a half hours to notice. Nobody was alerted when the root task failed, so add an error notification. A change in AWS broke Snowflake without anyone on the Snowflake side knowing, so integration changes need a review route. And finance noticed first, which is exactly what chapter seven's freshness alert was meant to prevent.

During the incident we needed task history from the last few hours. For the monthly cost review in chapter eight, we needed a whole month. Those questions need different sources, because operational evidence in Snowflake trades freshness against history. The information schema has no latency at all: it reflects what is happening right now. But it keeps only days to months of history, depending on the function, and it covers one database at a time. That makes it right for an incident in progress. The account usage views in the shared Snowflake database keep a full year, cover the whole account, and include objects that have since been dropped. But they lag behind, from forty-five minutes to about three hours depending on the view. That makes them right for trends, audits and cost reviews, and wrong for a live incident, where today's failure may not have arrived yet. The third source is event tables, which hold logs and traces written by your own procedures, functions and applications: the evidence from inside your code. Access needs thought too. By default, only account admin can read account usage. Rather than handing that role to operators, grant them the Snowflake database roles designed for it, such as usage viewer, or governance viewer for auditors. Then match the source to the question.

When data is lost, the first question is which mechanism can bring it back, and who holds the key. There are four. Time Travel, from chapter three, is self-service: you query, clone or undrop, as far back as the table's retention, up to ninety days for permanent tables. Fail-safe adds seven more days, but only Snowflake support can recover from it, on a best-effort basis that can take hours or days. It is a last resort, never part of a recovery plan. Clones give you a restore point at the moment you take one, as we did before the release, and they share storage with the source until the data diverges. And backup sets, which became generally available in late twenty twenty-five, take scheduled backups that expire on a policy, and can cover more than tables. The boundaries matter as much as the mechanisms. Transient tables, like our raw batch table, have no Fail-safe at all. Iceberg tables on your own storage depend on your own cloud backups. And there is a subtle difference in who can undo protection. An administrator can shorten Time Travel to zero, deliberately or by mistake. A backup set with a retention lock cannot be deleted by anyone, not even account admin, which is what regulators often require. That lock needs Business Critical edition and is irreversible, so it is a decision to take carefully, because locked backups are undeletable storage you pay for. Finally, rehearse. A recovery path nobody has actually tried is a guess, so restore into a scratch database on a schedule and check the row counts.

Recovering a dropped table is one thing. Recovering from a whole Region being unavailable is another, and it needs a second account in another Region, kept current by replication. Snowflake offers two kinds of group. A replication group copies databases, and other objects, to a secondary account on a schedule, and the secondary is always read-only. That is available from Standard edition. A failover group can also promote the secondary to become the primary, and Client Redirect lets one connection URL follow it, so clients reconnect without changing configuration. Failover groups need Business Critical edition. Here is an honest finding for our retailer. PROD was created on Enterprise in chapter one. It can replicate to a disaster recovery account today, but it cannot fail over until its edition changes. A business continuity plan has to start from facts like that. Then come the objectives. The recovery point objective is how much data you could lose. With a thirty-minute schedule, a secondary can be up to twice that behind, so up to an hour. The recovery time objective depends on far more than Snowflake: the landing bucket is still in the failed Region, the IAM trust must cover the new account, and the orchestrator and BI tools must point at the right place. Failback is a second migration. And a failover that has never been drilled is unknown.

The last kind of incident is the one nobody wants: security and cost. Both are handled the same way, from runbooks written in advance, with a named owner for every step, and both start with containment before investigation. On the ninth of October, the loader service user is seen connecting from an IP address nobody recognises. Its private key has leaked. Step one is containment: disable the user, which stops new sessions immediately, and add the address to the network policy's blocked list. Step two is rotation. Snowflake users have two key slots, so the platform team adds a new public key in the second slot, moves the job to the new private key, and removes the old one, without the pipeline being down for longer than necessary. Step three is scope: login history and access history from chapter nine show exactly what that session read. If personal data was read, step four involves the data owner and legal. And the last step is learning: why could a service user connect from that address at all? A user-level network policy would have prevented it. A cost incident has the same shape. The BI warehouse has run three clusters all weekend. Cap it first, then find the cause, a dashboard refreshing every ten seconds, and fix it with its owner. Runbooks only work if written before, owned by name, and rehearsed.

Everything in this course has been a part. In this final chapter we put the parts together into one data product and ask whether the whole design holds up. A data product is defined by who reads it and what they were promised. The tables follow from that, not the other way round. Our retail product has four consumers. Finance wants revenue no more than thirty minutes old during trading hours. Store managers want their own store's orders, and only theirs, ready by seven in the morning. The York partner gets daily figures through a versioned share. And data science wants order history with customers as they were at the time, the type two dimension from chapter five. Notice how different those promises are. Turning them into requirements means making each one precise. Freshness is a number and a window, never just real time. And the strictest consumer must not dictate every table's schedule: finance's thirty minutes applies to revenue, not to reference data that changes once a month. Contracts and access are requirements too: the v2 definition, the store row policy, the masked email. Finally, ownership is written down once. The owner runs the product and fixes it when it breaks. The steward, here finance, owns what revenue means. Consumers agree the contract, and a change to it is negotiated with them, not announced to them.

There is more than one way to build this product end to end, and each earlier chapter showed a piece of each. Option A is the full rebuild: copy the day's files every night, then recompute the results from scratch. Option B is streams and tasks: Snowpipe loads files as they land, and a task merges the changes the stream reports. Option C is dynamic tables: Snowpipe again, then results declared as queries with a target lag. None of them is the modern answer in general. Judge them on the requirements from the last section. Freshness: A is daily, B is as often as its schedule, C follows its target lag. What you own: A is one query; B is offsets and a merge you must get right; C is only the result query. Late customer changes: a rebuild absorbs them naturally, a stream and merge needs the source sequence guard from chapter six, and a dynamic table can only express that rule as a query. Recovery and cost differ too. So RETAILCO chooses per input, not per platform. Orders use dynamic tables, because finance needs thirty minutes. Customer changes use a stream and a guarded merge, because they arrive late and out of order. And reference data, small and rarely changing, is simply rebuilt every night.

Before Snowflake, finance read revenue from an older on-premises warehouse, which we'll call legacy D W. Moving finance across is a migration, and migrations fail when they happen all at once. So this one is staged. First, a parallel run: for fourteen days both systems build revenue from the same inputs. Second, reconcile every store and every day. A difference is not automatically a bug in the new system, but every one must be explained. For example, the legacy warehouse never netted refunds, so it is compared against the first version of the revenue view, not the second. Third, move consumers one at a time: finance's dashboard first, then the partner's export, which the share replaces. Only after thirty quiet days is the legacy path retired. Acceptance is evidence, agreed before the parallel run starts: equal row counts, totals within a penny, freshness within thirty minutes, and the policy matrix passing. The figures on screen are illustrative. The reconciliation query is written to return no rows when everything matches. And know where rollback stops being cheap. While the legacy warehouse is still loading, rolling back is just pointing consumers back. Once it stops loading, there is nothing current to go back to, and the only way is forward.

A design is really a series of choices, and choices are forgotten faster than code. A decision record keeps each one with its reason. A good record has five parts. The requirement, and whose it is. The decision. The alternatives that were rejected, with the reason for each, because the rejected options are exactly what the next engineer will propose. The evidence, which should be a query or a measurement, not an opinion. And the condition that would make you revisit it. When a decision changes, you don't edit the old record; you write a new one that supersedes it, so the history of reasoning survives. ADR four chose a nightly rebuild for orders; when finance asked for thirty-minute revenue, ADR eleven superseded it. Here is the record for finance's freshness. The requirement is revenue at most thirty minutes old during trading hours. The decision is a dynamic table with a fifteen-minute target lag. An hourly rebuild was rejected because it could be an hour old and rescans history. Streams and tasks were rejected because they give the same freshness with more code to own. The evidence is the refresh history from chapter seven. And it will be revisited if finance needs under five minutes, or if the monthly budget comes under pressure. The course has already made several decisions like this. In performance, a range predicate instead of a clustering key, from chapter eight. In governance, one row policy rather than a view per store. In cost, a resource monitor. In recovery, replication now, with failover waiting on an edition change.

This course covered the core of an analytical data product on Snowflake: from a first query, through access, tables, loading, transformation, change processing, pipelines, performance, governance and operations, to the architecture as a whole. Several surfaces lie beyond it, and each deserves its own study. Iceberg tables keep data in the open Iceberg format, so engines such as Spark can read the same tables. The first question there is which catalog manages them. Hybrid tables serve transactional, row-at-a-time work, with primary keys that are actually enforced. Native Apps package logic and data into an app that other accounts install, and can run containers through Snowpark Container Services. And Cortex AI brings AI functions, such as AI complete and AI classify, into SQL. Adopt one only when a requirement calls for it, and check its limits first. Hybrid tables, for example, cannot feed streams or dynamic tables, and cannot be shared, so they would not slot into our pipeline unchanged. Meanwhile, RETAILCO has its own backlog, in order of risk: an alert on task failure, so finance is never the monitoring system again. A decision on edition, so the disaster recovery account can actually take over. Recovery drills. And retiring the legacy warehouse. Following worked examples is not the same as running production, and the next step is practice.
